proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the monochromatic-circumcenter hypothesis. Assume for contradiction that both colors occur, and choose opposite-colored points O and G. Let r=dist(O,G)>0 and choose s=r/4, so 0<s<r/2. By the elementary circle lemma, choose seven distinct points on the circle centered at G with radius s. By the local exclusion lemma L8, that circle cannot contain five points of color f(G), so among the seven points at least three must have the other color, namely f(O). Those three distinct same-colored points lie on one circle centered at G, so L1 forces the center G itself to have color f(O), contradicting the choice of O and G as opposite-colored. Therefore both colors cannot occur, and the coloring is constant. The key improvement over the rejected attempts is that the heavy geometry is localized in L8 and uses the actual 2-coloring hypotheses; no false global statement about arbitrary circumcenter-closed subsets is used. Internally, L8 is supported by the corrected transfer lemma L3, the exact two-circle intersection lemma L4, the finite generic-position support configuration L5, the circle bound L2, and the pigeonhole lemma L6.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying the root hypothesis: for every noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A).
steps.trivial_justification: This is the assumption of the root theorem, specialized to an arbitrary coloring f.

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that f takes both colors. Then there exist points O,G in R^2 such that f(O) ≠ f(G).
steps.trivial_justification: To prove the coloring is constant, it suffices to rule out the possibility that both colors occur. If both colors occur, choose one point O of one color and one point G of the other color.

steps.derives: The points O and G are distinct, so r := dist(O,G) satisfies r > 0.
steps.trivial_justification: If O=G then f(O)=f(G), contradicting A2. Distinct points in the Euclidean plane have positive distance, hence r>0.

steps.derives: Define s := r/4. Then 0 < s < r/2.
steps.trivial_justification: Since r>0, dividing by 4 gives s>0, and r/4<r/2 is immediate from positivity of r.

steps.derives: There exist seven pairwise distinct points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5,X_6,X_7 on Circle(G,s).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L7 to the point G and the positive radius s from A4.

steps.derives: Among the seven points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5,X_6,X_7, at most four have color f(G).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L8 applies because A1 supplies the root hypothesis, A2 supplies the opposite-colored points O and G, and A4 gives 0<s<dist(O,G)/2. Therefore Circle(G,s) cannot contain five pairwise distinct points all of color f(G). Since the seven X_i are pairwise distinct and lie on that circle by A5, at most four of them can have color f(G).

steps.derives: At least three of the seven points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5,X_6,X_7 have color different from f(G). Since the only two colors are red and green and f(O) ≠ f(G), those at least three points all have color f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: There are seven total points and at most four have color f(G), so at least three do not have color f(G). Because the codomain of f is exactly the two-element set {red,green}, any point not colored f(G) must be colored with the other color, namely f(O) from A2.

Choose three distinct points among the seven X_i that have color f(O), whose existence is given by A7 and whose distinctness is inherited from A5. These three points lie on Circle(G,s) by A5. Applying L1 with center G and radius s shows that the center G must also have color f(O).
A2 states f(O) ≠ f(G), while A8 states f(G)=f(O).

steps.derives: Therefore f does not take both colors. Hence there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: From the contradiction, both colors cannot occur. Since every point has one of the two colors red or green, the image of f is a singleton subset of {red,green}. Let c be its unique element. Then every point P satisfies f(P)=c.

steps.derives: For every function f : R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all noncollinear points A,B,C in R^2 with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 fixed an arbitrary coloring f under the root hypothesis, and A10 established exactly the desired conclusion for that arbitrary f.
